Kay had stated it plainly, her words carrying the weight of an unshakeable truth: they could not raise mixed-race children in the American South. The declaration hung in the air long after she spoke it, a heavy, invisible boundary drawn over the blueprint of their future. 

That warning echoed in the narrator’s mind as they crossed the border into Kentucky. The shifting landscape—a blur of rolling hills and winding highways—felt less like a scenic drive and more like a steady descent into hostile territory. The ambient tension snapped into sharp focus when a rusted pickup truck pulled out in front of them. Stretched boldly across its back windshield was a massive Confederate flag, its faded red, white, and blue emblem catching the glare of the afternoon sun.

The sight of the flag hit the narrator like an electric shock, immediately igniting a visceral, violent fury. A wave of dark aggression flooded their thoughts. For a terrifying second, the narrator imagined pit-maneuvering the truck off the shoulder, ramming its bumper, or dragging the driver out onto the hot asphalt—anything to obliterate the symbol and the systemic threat it represented. It was an instinctive, protective rage, desperate to destroy the hostility before it could harm them.

Gripping the wheel until their knuckles turned white, the narrator pulled out to pass the vehicle, bracing for a confrontation. But as their car drew parallel to the truck, the expectation of malice met an unsettling reality. Sitting in the open bed of the pickup was a young boy, no older than seven or eight. As the narrator’s car passed, the child didn't offer a scowl or a hateful gesture. Instead, his face lit up, and he gave them a bright, cheerful smile, waving his hand with unreserved childhood warmth.

The dissonance of the moment was jarring, leaving a lingering, sour taste in the air. The narrator passed the truck and pulled back into the lane, completely disarmed yet deeply unsettled. Beside them, the tension had not broken. Kay sat rigidly in the passenger seat, staring straight ahead through the windshield. Her jaw was set, and her hands were drawn tightly against her lap, squeezed into trembling, bloodless fists. The boy’s innocent smile had done nothing to soften the encounter; if anything, the surreal contrast had only confirmed her worst fears, hardening her resolve about the world they were driving through.
outputs.L4:
The August heat in rural South Carolina had a weight to it, heavy and wet, clinging to the asphalt of Highway 17 like grease. In the backseat of our station wagon, the air conditioning blew a feeble cool mist over my two children. I watched them in the rearview mirror—my daughter, with her deep golden skin and a crown of tight brown curls, asleep against the window; my son, a shade lighter, humming softly to a song only he could hear. 

To parent mixed-race children in the American South is to live in a state of perpetual, ambient recalibration. You learn to read the room, the gas station, the roadside diner, scanning for the quiet threats that might shatter the fragile sanctuary you try to build around their innocence. It is an exhausting geometry of vigilance, measuring distance, tone, and intent in places where history is never truly past.

Then, he pulled out from a side road ahead of us. 

It was a rusted, late-nineties Ford F-150, its bumper caked in red clay. Stretched across the entirety of its rear windshield was a faded, sun-bleached Confederate flag, its crimson and blue crisscross stark against the blinding afternoon light. 

Instantly, my stomach lurked into a tight knot. The muscles in my forearms hardened, hands gripping the leather of the steering wheel until my knuckles turned white. My instinct, honed by years of protective hyper-awareness, demanded distance. *Back off,* it said. *Let him pull away.* 

But a darker, more defiant impulse took hold—a desperate, protective urge to know the face of the potential threat. I wanted to see who sat behind that emblem of historical violence. I needed to size up the danger, to read the eyes of the person who drove around wrapped in a symbol that denied my children’s right to exist unmolested in their own skin.

I stepped on the gas. The station wagon’s engine groaned, accelerating up the left lane. 

As we pulled alongside the truck, time seemed to stretch into a agonizing slow-motion. My eyes darted from the road to the truck’s cab, heart hammering a frantic rhythm against my ribs. I braced myself for what I had conditioned myself to expect: a sneer, a hardened glare, a middle finger, or the casual, practiced hostility of a man comfortable in his dominance.

We came abreast of the passenger side. 

Sitting in the front seat was not a towering, grizzled partisan of the Old South, but a small boy. He couldn't have been more than seven years old. He wore a faded baseball cap pulled low over light blond hair, his knees propped up against the dashboard. 

As our windows aligned, the boy turned. He looked directly at me, then down at my children in the back. There was no hesitation, no learned suspicion in his face. Instead, a bright, gap-toothed smile burst across his freckled features. He raised a small hand and waved with a vigorous, unreserved warmth—the pure, indiscriminate friendliness of a child eager to connect with a passing stranger on a long, boring drive. Beside him, the driver, an older man who looked like his grandfather, kept his eyes fixed firmly on the highway ahead, entirely oblivious to the transaction.

I froze. My breath caught in my throat.

I didn't wave back. I couldn't. The station wagon surged ahead, cutting back into the right lane and leaving the battered Ford behind in the heat haze.

Inside our car, a heavy, disorienting silence settled over us. My chest throbbed with a tangled mess of emotions: shame for my own defensive reflex, relief that there was no immediate danger, and a profound, aching sorrow. 

The boy’s innocent smile had not erased the flag behind his head; if anything, it made the symbol more tragic, highlighting how seamlessly hate is passed down, disguised as heritage, ready to inherit a mind so currently filled with light. The interaction offered no easy closure, only the disarming, bruised complexity of the South—a place where brutal history and sudden, unexpected grace live side-by-side in the very same truck, leaving those of us navigating its roads suspended forever between fear and hope.

There is a quiet magic to late afternoon in **Kentucky**, the kind that settles like a warm blanket over the rolling pastures and limestone creeks. As the sun begins its slow descent, painting the sky in shades of amber and pale violet, **Kay** steps out onto the wide, wooden porch of her family’s homestead. 

For **Kay**, this landscape is more than just a place on a map; it is a tapestry woven from generations of memory and tradition. Deep in the heart of the **South**, where the pace of life slows to match the rhythmic hum of evening cicadas, she finds a sense of peace that nowhere else can offer. 

She pours two glasses of sweet tea over ice, the condensation glistening in the humid air. The air carries the rich scents of damp earth, blooming wild clover, and the faint, sweet char from a distant bourbon distillery. Looking out across the emerald hills—the signature beauty of the Bluegrass State—**Kay** watches a pair of thoroughbreds trace the fence line, their sleek coats catching the last rays of sunlight.

To live in the **South** is to understand the value of storytelling, hospitality, and home. **Kay** embodies all three. Whether she is tending to her sprawling garden, hosting neighbors for a weekend porch-picking session filled with fiddle and banjo melodies, or simply watching the fog roll in over the Appalachian foothills, she carries the gentle strength of her roots. 

As twilight deepens and the fireflies begin their silent, flickering dance across the lawn, **Kay** takes a slow sip of her tea and leans back in her rocking chair. In the quiet warmth of a **Kentucky** night, she knows there is nowhere else in the world she would rather be.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a literary fiction scene about a couple driving into Kentucky, dealing with the heavy tension of discussing raising mixed-race children in the South while encountering symbolic Southern imagery like humidity and a truck with a Confederate flag.
counterfactuals.output:
The air changed the moment they crossed the Brent Spence Bridge. It was as if the Ohio River were a seam holding two distinct climates together, and south of it, the world had been wrapped in a damp, warm washcloth. 

Maya rolled her window down an inch, just enough to test it. The humidity pressed in immediately—thick, sweet with diesel and river mud, carrying the heavy, green scent of bruised leaves. It settled on her skin like a second shirt. She pulled the window back up, but the glass was already fogging around the edges.

"AC’s struggling," Julian said. His eyes remained fixed on the gray stretch of I-75. His knuckles were pale against the dark leather of the steering wheel.

"It’s fine," Maya said. She rested her right hand on the swell of her belly. Six months along, the baby had begun to feel less like an abstraction and more like an anchor, holding her down to the seat, to the car, to the choice they had made.

They had been driving for four hours, but the silence had only grown heavy in the last twenty miles, ever since the suburbia of southern Ohio gave way to the rolling, limestone-capped hills of Northern Kentucky. 

"My mom called while you were in the rest stop," Julian said, his voice carefully neutral. "She asked if we’d picked out paint for the nursery yet. I told her we were waiting until we unpacked."

Maya stared out at the wall of kudzu smothering the pines along the embankment. "Did she ask about the school district again?"

Julian cleared his throat, a small, tight sound. "She’s just curious. She doesn't mean anything by it."

"It’s a valid question, Jules," Maya said softly. She didn't turn to look at him. "It’s the only question that matters."

"We talked about this. Lexington has good pockets. The university brings in—"

"Pockets," she repeated. The word tasted dry, despite the damp air leaking through the dashboard vents. "We’re talking about where our kid goes to third grade, Julian. Where he walks home from the bus stop. I don't want him living in a pocket. I want him to be able to breathe outside of it."

"He’ll be fine," Julian said, but the assertion lacked conviction; it was a prayer uttered by someone who wasn't sure he believed in the deity he was addressing. He reached across the console to cover her hand, his palm cool from the air conditioner. "We’re going to give him a good life, Maya. Space. A yard. A house we could actually afford."

"Space for who?" she asked, her voice dropping an octave, flat and even. 

Julian didn't answer. The road dipped, and traffic slowed to a crawl behind a line of orange construction cones. The heat outside seemed to radiate off the asphalt in shimmering, visible waves, bowing the horizon.

A diesel engine rumbled to their left, high and heavy. Maya looked up. 

A lifted Ford F-250 had pulled up alongside them, idling in the adjacent lane. Its tires were coated in dried red clay, and the chrome bumper was spotted with rust. Draped across the entirety of the back glass was a faded, grease-stained Confederate flag, its red cloth bleached pink by years of high-noon sun, the blue saltire fraying at the corners where it caught the wind.

Inside the truck, the driver’s arm rested on the open window frame—red-skinned, hairy, holding a melting cup of gas station ice. He didn't look at them. He was just sitting there, suspended in the same heat, listening to the crackle of a talk-radio host complaining about tax rates.

Julian’s eyes darted to the side mirror, then back to the bumper in front of them. He shifted his grip on the wheel, his shoulders rising a fraction of an inch. He didn't say anything, but his silence grew thin and brittle, like ice over a pond.

Maya watched the flag. It was unremarkable in its presence—not a grand statement here, just part of the local flora, like the chicory growing wild in the ditches or the rusted tin roofs of the tobacco barns rotting in the fields. That was what made her stomach tighten. It wasn't an anomaly; it was background noise. 

She thought of the boy growing inside her—the combination of Julian’s pale, burn-prone skin and her own deep brown, the hair that would inevitably confuse the local barbers, the way his name would read on a job application in twenty years. Julian saw a countryside of horse farms and fresh air; she saw a landscape mapped by invisible, rigid lines, where a child could cross from safety into suspicion by walking down the wrong dirt road.

"Jules," she whispered.

"I see it," he said softly. He didn't look at the truck, but his jaw was clamped so tight a muscle twitched beneath his ear.

"He’s going to look like me," she said. It was the first time she had said it out loud, though they had both known it. "If he takes after my father’s side, he’s going to be dark. You know that, right?"

"Maya, please. Don't do this right now."

"I have to do it right now," she said, her voice rising, though she kept her eyes fixed on the frayed edges of the red banner idling next to them. "Because when we get off this highway, you get to just be a guy buying a house in Kentucky. And I have to figure out how to teach a child to survive the place you chose for us."

Julian swallowed hard. He looked at her then, his blue eyes wide, mapped with red veins from the long drive, filled with a helpless, desperate kind of love that made her chest ache. He wanted so badly for the world to be simple, for his good intentions to be a thick enough coat to protect them all from the rain.

"I’m here," he said, his voice breaking slightly. "I’m in it with you."

"You are," she agreed, placing her hand over his on the console, feeling the heat of his skin against hers. "But you’re standing on the dry side of the glass."

Ahead of them, the orange cones ended. The brake lights of the truck flickered off, and the big V8 engine roared, spouting a dark puff of exhaust into the humid air before pulling away down the incline. 

Julian pressed the gas. The car moved forward, rolling into the green, heavy belly of the state, carrying them toward a home that was already waiting, framed by trees older than the conflict, roots sunk deep into the dark, damp earth.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short, tense driving scene set in the rural South that subverts the narrator's expectations about a passing truck with a Confederate flag.
counterfactuals.output:
The humidity hung like a wet wool blanket over State Route 9, a two-lane ribbon of decaying asphalt swallowed whole by the pine barrens of southern Georgia. Dusk was bleeding into black, and my cell phone had been bouncing between *Searching...* and *No Service* for the last twenty miles. 

Then came the headlights. 

They appeared in my rearview mirror like a pair of angry suns, high-mounted and blindingly bright. I shifted my rental sedan closer to the fog line, expecting a quick pass. Instead, the vehicle surged up until its steel bumper was inches from my trunk. 

Engine roaring, it hovered there. In the harsh glare reflected in my side mirror, I caught the silhouetted lifted suspension, the oversized mud tires, and, plastered across the back glass, the unmistakable crossed red bars of a faded Confederate flag.

My pulse spiked, thick and hot in my throat. I was a city guy in a blue-state rental, isolated on a dark country road, and being aggressively tailgated by a truck that seemed tailored for a local nightmare. 

I sped up. Seventy. Seventy-five. The sedan’s tiny four-cylinder engine whined in protest. 

The truck matched my speed instantly. It blared its horn—a deafening train-horn blast that shattered the quiet night—and flashed its high beams wildly. 

*Don’t stop,* I told myself, my knuckles stark white against the steering wheel. *Just keep driving.*

The truck suddenly swung into the left lane, its massive tires spraying gravel against my passenger door. It pulled side-by-side with me. I kept my eyes locked on the road ahead, refusing to look into the cab, terrified of whatever gesture or weapon might be aimed my way. 

The truck didn't just pass. It swerved violently back into my lane, cut off my nose, and slammed on its brakes.

Red tail lights flooded my cabin. Rubber shrieked. I stomped the brake pedal with both feet, my seatbelt cutting painfully across my chest as the sedan skidded to a stop, missing the truck's rear bumper by inches. 

Trapped. The road was lined by dense, ditch-lined forest on both sides. 

I scrambled to lock the doors. My heart knocked frantically against my ribs. In the truck's cab ahead, the driver’s side door swung open. 

A tall figure stepped out into the beam of my headlights. He wore a grease-stained mesh cap, work boots, and a heavy flannel shirt. In his right hand, he carried something long and metallic. A iron pipe? A pry bar? 

He started toward my car, walking fast. 

I pressed my back into the seat, looking desperately for a gap to reverse, but the road was too narrow, the darkness too absolute. The man reached my window and slapped the glass with the palm of his hand.

"Hey!" he yelled. "Roll it down! Roll it down right now!"

I cracked the window less than an inch, my voice trembling. "Leave me alone. I'm calling the police."

"Call whoever you want, but you need to get out of the car!" the man barked. He gestured frantically with the metal object—a heavy-duty flashlight. "Look at your hood, man!"

I blinked, forcing myself to look past his face. 

Wisps of thick, black smoke were pouring out from beneath the edges of my rental's hood. A faint, angry orange glow was blooming underneath the engine block. 

"Your fuel line must’ve ruptured!" the man shouted over the crackle of sudden flames. "It caught on your manifold! I’ve been trying to pull you over for three miles before the whole damn thing goes up!"

Before I could process his words, the man reached around, hit the latch through the cracked window, pulled my door open, and grabbed me by the front of my jacket. He yanked me out of the car with terrifying strength, dragging me twenty yards down the asphalt just as a soft *whoomph* erupted behind us. A wall of heat slapped the back of my neck as the engine bay burst into full, roaring flames.

I fell to my knees on the gravel shoulder, gasping, staring at the blazing wreck of the sedan. 

The driver dropped down beside me, chest heaving. He clapped a heavy hand on my shoulder. 

"You alright, buddy?" he asked, his southern drawl thick and genuinely anxious. "You hit your head or anything?"

I stared at him, speechlessness washing over me. "I... I thought you were—"

"I was trying to warn ya," he said, turning to rush back to his truck. "Hold tight! I got an extinguisher in the bed, but I'm calling the volunteer fire dept on the CB!"

He ran back to the lifted pickup, the faded flag on the glass gleaming under the firelight, as he pulled a fire extinguisher from the truck bed and charged straight toward the heat to fight a fire that wasn't his.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a vignette focusing on racial tension and internal monologue during a road trip. Use rich sensory details like sweat, sunburned skin, and sharp bones, and include a moment where the narrator has violent intrusive thoughts before passing another vehicle.
counterfactuals.output:
The sun had turned my left arm into a strip of raw bacon. Through the driver’s side window, the wind felt less like a breeze and more like an open industrial oven, baking the sunburned skin until it felt tight enough to split. Sweat gathered in the notch of my collarbone, pooling hot and sour before trailing down my ribs, where my sharp bones pressed against the thin, cracked vinyl of the driver’s seat. Every bump in State Route 9 was a bruised hip bone grinding against the chassis.

I had been stuck behind the rusted Ford F-150 for six miles. 

It was a slow, deliberate crawl—forty-two in a fifty-five. The truck’s rear glass was slapped with a faded Confederate cross and a sticker reading *TRY THAT IN A SMALL TOWN*. In the truck’s side mirror, I could see the driver’s eyes: pale, shaded by a stained mesh cap, flicking up every few seconds to lock onto mine. He knew I was there. He knew I was a dark face in an unfamiliar sedan with out-of-state plates, fifty miles from any interstate, surrounded by endless walls of suffocating loblolly pines.

My hands tightened on the wheel. My knuckles turned white, the skin stretched so thin the sharp bones beneath looked ready to break through. 

*He’s taking his time,* I thought. *He wants me to get impatient. He wants me to cross the line so he can find a reason.*

The heat in the cabin was sickening. The air conditioner blew dry, tepid dust. A droplet of sweat stung my left eye, but I didn't take a hand off the wheel to wipe it. Hyper-vigilance had turned my spine to iron. *Keep your hands at ten and two. Don't look aggressive. If he pulls over, don't reach for the glovebox.* The mentally rehearsed script of survival played on a loop, the same one my father had taught me, the one his father had taught him. 

Then the truck tapped its brakes. Just a flash of red light. No animal on the road. No turn coming up. Just a flex. A silent reminder of who owned this stretch of asphalt.

A sudden, white-hot spike shot through my brain—a violent, ugly intrusive thought that smelled like burnt rubber and iron. 

*Flooring it.* 

In my mind, I didn't just pull around him; I yanked the wheel to the right, burying my front bumper into his driver-side quarter panel. I imagined the violent, satisfying crunch of metal, the truck losing traction, flipping side-over-side into the drainage ditch, smashing through the tree line. I wanted to see the glass shatter. I wanted to feel the shockwave of the impact shudder through my wrists, to rip that smirk off his face and bury him in the clay under the pines where nobody would hear him bleed. I wanted to carve my name into this godforsaken highway with his wreckage.

The fantasy was so vivid my foot actually twitched toward the gas pedal, my pulse thumping like a war drum against my ear drums. My skin burned hotter, the phantom smell of smoke filling my lungs.

Then, the solid yellow line melted into a dotted one. 

The heat of the moment snapped like a dry twig, leaving behind a cold, sickening wave of shame and adrenaline. My heart hammered against my ribs. 

I cut the wheel to the left. 

I stomped on the accelerator. The sedan’s four-cylinder engine shrieked in protest, dragging us out into the open lane. As I pulled alongside the truck, time slowed. I refused to turn my head, but in my peripheral vision, I felt his gaze—heavy, contemptuous, waiting for a reaction. My jaw clamped so hard my back teeth aching, sweat dripping off my chin onto my chest.

I passed him. 

The sedan surged ahead, cutting back into the right lane. In the rearview mirror, the truck shrank, a fading rusted square against the shimmering heat haze of the road. I let out a long, ragged breath, my sunburned arm thrumming with a dull, furious ache as the empty road swallowed me whole.

"We shouldn't raise a mixed baby down here," Kay said, her palm resting flat against the gentle swell of her stomach as the rusted sign welcoming them to Kentucky flashed past in the twilight. 

Marcus kept his hands at ten and two on the steering wheel, his knuckles slightly white, though he forced a soft, reassuring smile. "It's just trees and rolling hills, Kay. My uncle’s place is quiet. Nobody’s going to bother us."

"Trees and rolling hills have memories," she murmured, watching the thick canopy of oak and pine swallow the last lingering orange of the sunset. The highway shrank from four lanes to two, winding deeper into the dark, unlit curves of the state route. 

Ten minutes later, the high beams appeared in the rearview mirror. 

They came out of nowhere, twin points of blinding white light that rose up fast over the crest of the hill behind them. Marcus adjusted the center mirror, wincing at the glare that filled the cabin of the sedan. 

"Tailgating," Marcus muttered. "Classic."

"Just let him pass," Kay said quietly. Her hand had tightened on the edge of the dashboard. Her phone sat in her lap; the screen displayed a single, depressing bar of signal that flickered and died as they sank deeper into the valley.

Marcus flicked his turn signal and pulled as far onto the narrow shoulder as the gravel allowed, slowing down to give the vehicle room to blow past. 

The vehicle didn't pass. It slowed down too, riding their bumper so close that Marcus couldn't even see the grille in his mirror—just the brutal, piercing halogen glow illuminating the dust motes dancing inside their own car.

"Marcus," Kay whispered, her voice tight. "He's not passing."

"I see him." Marcus tapped the brakes—just a light warning touch. 

The response behind them was immediate. The driver flashed their high beams three times in rapid, aggressive succession, illuminating the interior of Marcus and Kay’s car like a stage light. In that brief, violent burst of light, Marcus’s dark skin and Kay’s pale profile were framed perfectly against the windows.

The roar of a heavy engine echoed off the surrounding rock faces. The vehicle—a lifted, midnight-blue pickup with oversized tires—swerved out into the oncoming lane. But instead of accelerating past, it matched their speed, traveling side-by-side with them at fifty miles an hour on a winding, two-lane road.

Kay turned her head slowly, almost terrified of what she’d see. The truck’s passenger window was rolled down. The cabin was dark, but she could make out the thick, squared shape of a man sitting in the passenger seat, staring straight down into their sedan. He didn't wave. He didn't gesture. He just watched them, his silhouette motionless against the backdrop of the passing trees.

"Don't look at them," Marcus said, his voice dropping an octave, trying to sound steady while his heart hammered against his ribs. 

"He's staring right at me, Marc," Kay choked out, pulling her seatbelt slightly looser across her belly, a instinctual, protective reflex. "Please. Speed up."

"If I speed up on these curves, we'll slide off the ridge." Marcus pressed his foot down slightly, the sedan’s four-cylinder engine whining in protest. 

The truck matched the acceleration effortlessly, its massive tires humming a low, menacing rhythm against the asphalt. Then, the truck began to drift right. 

Inch by inch, the heavy steel quarter-panel of the pickup closed the distance between them. 

"He's pushing us!" Kay gasped, her hands flying to the dashboard as the sedan’s tires caught the rough rumble strip on the edge of the road. The car vibrated violently, a loud *thrum-thrum-thrum* rattling the frame. 

Marcus gripped the wheel with everything he had, fighting the pull of the gravel. "Hold on!" 

He slammed on the brakes. 

The sedan shuddered, nose-diving as the tires screeched against the dark pavement. The pickup, caught off guard by the sudden drop in speed, shot ahead fifty yards. 

For a fraction of a second, relief washed over the cabin—until the pickup's red brake lights flared angrily in the dark. The truck didn't just slow down; it skidded to a complete sideways stop, blocking both lanes of the narrow road, its long body sealing off the highway like a steel barricade.

Marcus stomped on the brake pedal, bringing the sedan to a halt just thirty feet from the truck’s exposed side panel. 

The engine of the sedan idled softly, a pathetic contrast to the deep, guttural rumble of the lifted truck. Out here, deep in the Kentucky dark, there were no streetlights, no passing cars, and no cell service. Just the twin beams of Marcus's headlights cutting through the rising fog, shining directly onto the faded bumper sticker on the back of the truck, and the driver’s side door slowly, deliberately swinging open.

Kay looked over at Marcus, her eyes wide, tears spilling silently down her cheeks. 

"Marcus," she whispered, her voice trembling in the dark. "What do we do?"
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a flash fiction piece where a driver and their partner encounter a beaten-up truck displaying a Confederate flag. Show the narrator's escalating dark thoughts toward the truck, contrasted sharply by a boy in the truck bed smiling and waving, which leaves the partner fuming.
counterfactuals.output:
The tailpipe of the Ford F-150 spat a thick, greasy plume of black soot directly onto our windshield. It was a rusted hulk of a thing, its rear bumper hanging by a prayer and a length of coat hanger wire. 

And there, stretched across the entirety of the back glass, was the faded, frayed cloth of a Confederate flag.

My hands tightened on the leather of the steering wheel. A hot, toxic itch began to creep up the back of my neck. I shifted into the left lane, preparing to pass, but the truck drifted lazily over the broken white line, cutting me off.

*Unconscious,* I thought. *Or deliberate.* 

My pulse drummed in my ears. I felt a dark, violent impulse spike in my chest. I imagined keeping my foot pinned to the gas, burying our bumper into their rusted tailgate. I wanted to feel the crunch of their cheap metal. I pictured the truck losing control, leaf springs snapping, tires gripping the gravel shoulder before pitching sideways into the sun-baked ditch. I wanted to see it roll. I wanted to see that rag torn to shreds in a cloud of dust and sparks, purging the highway of its ugliness. 

"Asshole," Sarah spat beside me, her voice trembling with a familiar, cold disgust. "Of course he’s driving like that."

I didn't answer. My mind was already somewhere worse. I was mapping out the physics of a PIT maneuver, feeling a terrifying, righteous malice. I wanted to pull up alongside the cab, force the driver to look at me, to see the absolute ruin I wished upon him. 

I pressed the accelerator. The engine hummed as we crept up beside the truck's bed. 

My eyes darted sideways, ready to burn holes into the driver. But my gaze caught on the bed of the truck first.

Sitting cross-legged amidst a mess of oil cans, a bald spare tire, and coiled rope was a little boy. He couldn't have been more than six. He wore an oversized, faded blue t-shirt and had grease smudges across his chubby cheeks. 

As our car aligned with the truck bed, the boy locked eyes with me. 

The dark fantasy in my head evaporated instantly, leaving behind a cold, hollow silence. 

The boy didn't look angry. He didn't look like an emblem of history's rot. He just looked like a kid getting a ride in the back of his dad’s truck on a hot summer afternoon. When he saw me watching him, his face lit up with a gap-toothed, radiant grin. He raised a small, dirty hand and waved frantically, his whole arm swinging in joyful, unprompted greeting.

My fingers slackened on the wheel. A involuntary, sheepish twitch caught the corner of my mouth. 

"Look at that," Sarah hissed, her face flushed red, knuckles white where she gripped the dashboard. She hadn't looked at the bed; her glaring eyes were locked strictly on the flag sticking out from the rear window. "They bring their trash out here just to rub it in everyone's face. God, I hate people like that. It makes my blood boil."

She slammed her hand against her knee, fuming, spouting a torrent of bitter fury into the quiet air of the car.

I didn't say anything. I just watched the boy in the rearview mirror as we pulled ahead, his tiny hand still waving at us until he faded into the heat shimmer of the road.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
